newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Worries expressed over Sri Lanka's war displaced.
newsitem.headline: Worries expressed over Sri Lanka's war displaced.

text.p: A major government offensive in Sri Lanka against Tamil rebels will put more pressure on northern refugee centres, already overcrowded with those made homeless by previous army campaigns, Tamil politicians and aid workers said.

"Reports reaching us say people are running like animals, driven from one village to another," said Veerasingham Anandasangari, vice-president of the Tamil United Liberation Front (TULF), a party represented in Sri Lanka's parliament.
"We are not yet sure of civilian casualties, but casualties of war are also those who have lost their homes and those who have no food," Anandasangari told Reuters on Monday.

Security forces, backed by artillery and tanks, last week launched a massive offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels' northern Wanni stronghold, aiming to reopen a land route that lies through rebel-held territory.
Troops want to capture a key road linking the government-held town of Vavuniya, 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo with Jaffna peninsula, about 100 km (60 miles) further north.
Jaffna, the former LTTE stronghold and the capital of a homeland they have been fighting for, is under government control.

The LTTE, fighting a 13-year-old war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east, control vast swathes of land in the Wanni in the island's northern region.
The rebels have accused the army of killing Tamil civilians and destroying property under the pretext of opening up a supply route.
"Tamil civilians are without doubt the prime targets of Sri Lanka's military forces," an LTTE statement said on Sunday.
Aid workers said the Wanni is home to some 600,000 people, about half of them living in refugee centres after being dislodged from previous battles.
Anandasangari said thousands of people have taken to the jungles after being made homeless from barrages of military artillery fired ahead of advancing troops.

Aid workers said Wanni's food stocks were strained by additional numbers joining the list of refugees and with government food supplies to the region grinding to a halt after the offensive began last Tuesday.
"Some solution will have to be found, because (food) stocks won't last forever," an official with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) told Reuters.
The ICRC has already started providing non-food relief to more than 400 newly displaced families, he said.
"From what we see right now, people seem to be coping. But if more people come on the roads and if the offensive goes on, there might be problems," the official added.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war, now in its 14th year. The rebels say the toll is higher.
